claims.text: Thermally activated Mg diffusion drives localized nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds in the metastable alloy.
Oxygen accelerates Mg-rich intermetallic formation by promoting localized oxidation along diffusion pathways and lowering the intermetallic nucleation barrier.
Lower temperature or an inert atmosphere limits Mg diffusion and oxidation sufficiently to retain the metastable solid-solution state.
Retention of the metastable state sustains corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Higher temperature under oxidizing conditions produces a diffusion-oxidation synergy that accelerates transformation to an intermetallic-dominated microstructure.
The accelerated transformation produces a continuous intermetallic network.
The high-temperature oxidizing condition produces a disrupted, thinner protective oxide scale.
A continuous intermetallic network and a disrupted oxide scale reduce corrosion and oxidation resistance.
The initial alloy is predominantly a metastable solid solution with minimal intermetallic phases.
The initial metastable state has robust corrosion and oxidation resistance.
The controlled comparison uses aging at 450°C and 600°C in Ar and air for 10 and 50 hours.
Oxygen adsorption at an alloy surface can initiate interfacial oxidation and selective oxide nucleation.
High-temperature alloy oxidation involves transport within the alloy, across the oxide-metal interface, and through the oxide layer.
Selective oxidation can deplete mobile alloying elements and alter oxide growth and near-surface microstructure.
At 600°C in air, Mg-rich intermetallic formation will be faster and more spatially uniform than at 450°C or in Ar.
At 600°C in air, the oxide scale will be thinner and less protective than under the lower-temperature or inert-atmosphere conditions.
Greater Mg-rich intermetallic formation and oxide-scale disruption will correlate with higher corrosion rates and poorer oxidation performance.
A lack of statistically significant microstructural and performance differences across atmosphere and temperature conditions would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says oxidation is suppressed in Ar, yet the predicted outcome says the 600°C air condition will have a thinner oxide scale than samples aged in inert Ar. Without specifying a pre-existing scale or a particular scale layer, greater oxygen exposure would not straightforwardly predict a thinner total scale than inert aging.
